prompts.title: Your country's recommendations dashboard
prompts.prompt:
Build this app. Follow the plan below; where it says nothing, keep it simple.

# UN human rights recommendations dashboard: Kenya

## Context

The user is a diplomat, an NGO officer or a staff member of a national human rights institution preparing a meeting, a briefing or a report on Kenya. They need three things in a row: how much the UN mechanisms have said, about what, and the exact paragraph with its UN document symbol. Today they open the Universal Human Rights Index, export to a spreadsheet and lose an hour; or they quote from memory. The dashboard must be trustworthy enough to be read out in a meeting: every number says how it was computed, every row links to the UN document. The data is `WORKSHOP_DATA.uhri`; the country is `WORKSHOP_DATA.uhri.country`, never hard-coded.

## What I found in the data

The numbers below come from the file I examined while planning; the participant's file differs, and the app must compute all of its own numbers.

- 2,264 records from 31 documents (18 treaty-body, 9 Special Procedures, 4 UPR), dated 2007–2026, with no records in some years. The top-level `count` is a **string** ("2264"): compare with `Number(count)`.
- `symbol`, `doc_url`, `date`, `year`, `body`, `mechanism`, `type` and `text` are filled in every record. `section` only in 450 (treaty bodies and one mandate); `themes` in 2,249; `sdgs` in 1,816 (448 have none); `affected_persons` in 1,856.
- `body` has 16 values; UPR is nearly half the records; some mandates have a handful (one has a single record).
- `type`: 1,791 Recommendations, 471 Concerns/Observations, 2 Other.
- 90 theme labels; a record carries several, so theme counts sum to more than the record count. The most frequent theme ("Reservations", 691) is a legacy label: sampled records under it, all from 2007–2013, had nothing to do with reservations. The app must show, not hide, this: a year range per theme and the sample check.
- Paragraph numbers sit at the start of `text`: "71. The Committee…" in treaty-body records (681 records in the file start that way), "144.43 Abolish…" in every UPR record; many Special Procedures records are lettered items "(g) Develop…" with no number.
- UPR texts end with a semicolon and one or more States in parentheses, sometimes with spaces inside, sometimes nested ("(Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of))"), sometimes several ("(Cabo Verde) (Slovenia) (Togo);"). 1,370 records end with a parenthesis, but treaty-body texts end with "(art. 15).", so State extraction must be limited to UPR.
- Texts run from 18 to about 2,500 characters (median about 230); a few 2007 records are chopped fragments joined with letters ("r) … r) …"). Two texts are exact duplicates of another record.

## The app, tab by tab

The app answers three questions, one per tab, and shows only what the open tab needs: **no view shows more than about seven things to click** (tabs, filter headings and buttons, not table rows or chart bars), and anything used rarely sits one click deeper. Three numbered tabs under the header, in this order.

**Header (always visible).** A monospace label "UHRI · Kenya", then the title in a large serif, "UN human rights recommendations and observations: Kenya". One line under it: source (`source`, linked to `source_url`), n records, n documents, first–last year, `built` date, and the hint "dated by document".

**Left rail: filters (always visible).** A narrow column headed "FILTERS" with "Clear all" at the right. Under it a big serif number, "n matching records" (`aria-live="polite"`, with "of N in the file"), and a thin red bar showing the share of the file. Active filters show as removable chips under the number. Every tab reads the same filtered set; all filters combine with AND. Three numbered headings, **each closed until clicked**, one open at a time (buttons with `aria-expanded`), shown on tabs 01 and 02; on 03 the rail keeps only the number, the bar and the chips.
- **01 Keyword**: a text box applied 300 ms after typing, hint "literal match, not synonyms".
- **02 Mechanism, body, type**: Mechanism (all / each value); Body or mandate (`body` values present in the chosen mechanism, each with its count); Type (all / each value present). A State select joins this heading when States are extracted.
- **03 Years and SDG**: Year from / to (two selects of the distinct years); SDG (goal number and name from `sdg_names`, only goals present in the data).

**01 Overview: what has the UN said, how much, and when?**
- A row of big serif numbers. The first tile counts **all records** in the file: recommendations, concerns/observations and any other `type`. Under the number, one line gives the breakdown per `type`, spelled as in the data. The Type filter (all / each `type` value present) starts on "all". Beside it: documents (distinct `symbol`) and years (min–max of `year`). Below, one tile per `mechanism` (records, documents, latest year, share of the filtered set). Every tile and figure has a one-line "How this is computed" note.
- FIG.01 "Ten most frequent themes among n filtered records": a horizontal Chart.js bar chart, bars ranked by value, count at the end of each bar. Clicking a bar adds that theme as a filter chip. Under the chart, a small table with the same ten rows: Theme | Records | % of filtered | Years (first–last year of the records carrying it), and the note that a record can carry several themes, so bars add up to more than n.
- FIG.02 "Records per year by mechanism": stacked bars for the current filter; every year from the first to the last appears, so empty years are visible gaps.
- Last, a closed heading **Every check (n)**, a button with `aria-expanded`: the "Check this dashboard" panel (section "How the app checks itself"), one line per check.

**02 Records: which paragraph says it, and in which UN document?**
- One search field across the top ("Search n records, e.g. torture"), the same box as 01 Keyword. The caption gives rows shown of rows matching.
- The table. Columns: Date | Body | Symbol (linked to `doc_url`, opens in a new tab) | Para. | First line (the first 120 characters, cut at a word, with "…"). **Recommending State** (UPR rows only): the State or States named in parentheses at the end of the text, as a column in the table and as a filter (a select listing every State found, with counts). On tab 01, a small "see the States" link in the UPR tile opens a short list in place ("Ten States that made most recommendations to Kenya") with counts for the current filter. Treaty-body and Special Procedures rows show a dash in this column. Rows are sorted by `date` descending, then `body`, then paragraph number ascending (numeric, so 10 follows 9), then the order in the file. The caption says "newest first"; clicking the Date header reverses it. Keyword matches are highlighted with `<mark>`. Fifty rows at a time with "Show 50 more".
- Clicking a row (or pressing Enter on it) expands it in place: the paragraph number large in red, the full `text` verbatim, never shortened or paraphrased; the labels (`themes`, `sdgs` with names, `sdg_targets`, `affected_persons`, `section` when present); the "Copy citation" button; and "Open the UN document". **Copy citation** copies the short form `symbol, para. N` (for example "CEDAW/C/AFG/CO/4, para. 54"). When no paragraph number was found in the text, it copies the symbol alone and the button's label says "(no paragraph number in this extract)".

**03 Method & export: how was this made, and how do I take it with me?**
- How each number is computed, in five or six plain sentences.
- "Download CSV of the current filter": the visible columns plus the full text and labels, preceded by comment lines with the country, source, build date, the filters applied and the row count, generated in the browser with a Blob URL. "Copy summary": a plain-text paragraph with the headline numbers and the ten themes, for pasting into notes.
- The data source, licence line and build date.

**Footer (always visible, one line, small monospace).** "Built on OHCHR UHRI data · n records · source link", plus a "Credits" line if any shelf code was used.

## How every number is computed

- **Headline total** = `records.length`. The breakdown counts records per `type`, using the values exactly as spelled in the data (there may be a small "Other" group).
- **Documents** = number of distinct `symbol`. **Years** = minimum and maximum `year`.
- **Filters.** Mechanism, body, type: exact match on the field. Year: `year` inclusive between the two selects. SDG: `sdgs.includes(goal)` with `goal` a number. Keyword: trimmed, lower-cased; every word must occur as a substring of `text` or `symbol`. The filtered set feeds the tiles, both charts, the table and the export.
- **Theme counts.** For each record in the filtered set, each value in `themes` counts once. Top ten by count, ties alphabetical. Percentage = count / filtered records, one decimal. Year range = min and max `year` of the filtered records carrying that theme.
- **Timeline** = records per `year` per `mechanism` in the filtered set, with zero for missing combinations.
- **Paragraph number** = the first match of `/^(\d{1,3}(?:\.\d{1,3})?)\.?\s/` on `text`; the captured group is the number ("71" or "144.43"); no match means no number.
- **Recommending State.** Only for `mechanism` === "Universal Periodic Review". Take the trailing run of parenthesised groups with the regular expression `/((?:\s*\((?:[^()]|\([^()]*\))*\))+)\s*[;.]?\s*$/` on `text`, then split that run into groups with `/\((?:[^()]|\([^()]*\))*\)/g`, strip the outer parentheses and trim. One group may hold a nested name such as "Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)"; several groups mean several States, and the record counts once for each. A group is accepted as a State only if it has no comma and at most 60 characters; otherwise the record gets "State not found". The text itself is never altered.
- **Citation** = `symbol` + ", para. " + paragraph number when one was found; otherwise `symbol`. UPR numbers keep their two-part form ("para. 144.43"). A small "Copied" confirmation appears for two seconds; the clipboard write is the only thing that leaves the page.
- **First line** = `text` up to 120 characters, cut at the last space before the limit, plus "…"; the full text is shown unchanged on expand.
- Nothing is estimated and no model is called. Every count is a loop over the records in JavaScript.

## How the app checks itself

The "Check this dashboard" panel, under the closed heading on the Overview tab, lists each check as one line: what was compared, the two values, and a pass mark or a red "check failed" with the values, never a hidden failure.

- **Record count.** `records.length` against `Number(uhri.count)`.
- **Partitions.** Counts per `mechanism`, per `body` and per `year` each sum to the record count.
- **Type partition.** The counts per `type` sum to the headline total.
- **Chart against table.** Each bar's value equals the count recomputed by a second loop over the filtered records; the ten rows under the chart show the same values; the largest bar is not larger than the filtered count.
- **Links.** Every record's `doc_url` starts with "https://docs.un.org/" and ends with its `symbol` (compared case-insensitively after decoding); the records that fail are listed.
- **Paragraph numbers.** Share of records with a number found, per mechanism; UPR is expected at 100%, and a lower figure is shown as a warning, not an error.
- **States found.** Number of UPR records with at least one State found, against the number of UPR records; the records without one are listed with their symbol, so the reader can see what the parentheses held instead.
- **Duplicates and gaps.** Distinct `id` equals the record count; the number of duplicate `text` values; records with no `themes`, no `sdgs`, no `affected_persons`, each shown as "not labelled".

## Edge cases and risks

- A filter that matches nothing: tiles show 0, the chart area shows "No records match" as text, the table caption says so; no error in the console.
- Years with no records appear as gaps on the timeline and are absent from the year selects; the from/to selects reject a reversed range by swapping it.
- `count` is a string; `sdgs` may be empty or missing; `section` is usually empty and is shown only when present; `type` may hold a small "Other" group.
- Theme bars add up to more than the record count; the note under the chart says so, and the percentages are of records, not of labels.
- A top theme may be a legacy label (in the file examined, the most frequent theme was wrong in every sampled record). The app never removes or renames a UN label; it shows the year range per theme and lets the reader judge a sample.
- A few UPR texts end with a parenthesis that is not a State (a list of examples, an article). The comma-and-length rule catches most; the check panel lists the rest. The State list is a count of recommendations, not of influence; two States can co-sponsor one line.
- Very short or chopped texts (2007 records) are shown as they are; the first-line column may then be the whole text.
- `date` is the document's date, not the date a recommendation was made or accepted; the header note says "dated by document".
- Keyword search is literal: "torture" does not find "ill-treatment". The hint under the box says so.
- Nothing leaves the browser except the clipboard write on "Copy"; there is no model call and no network request.

## Design and accessibility

What this app adds to the studio look and its accessibility:
- Red (#9b2335) also marks the share bar in the rail, the bars of FIG.01 (at 80%) and the large paragraph number in an open row. Big serif numbers: the matching count in the rail and the headline numbers on tab 01.
- Mechanism colours only on the tile dots and in FIG.02 (UPR #c2410c, Treaty bodies #0f766e, Special Procedures #7c3aed), always with a label or legend.
- Figure titles say what is counted and for which filter, with a "Source" line under each figure.
- Charts follow "Data visualisation: charts (formatting, labels, bar charts)" (UK Government Analysis Function): horizontal bars, ranked, horizontal text, and a table under the chart because a well-structured table can be as powerful as a chart.
- Tables follow "Data visualisation: tables" (Analysis Function): thousands separators, the same precision in a column, the source under the table.
- Keyboard: tabs are a `role="tablist"` with arrow-key navigation; filter headings and expandable rows are buttons with `aria-expanded`; the matching count is `aria-live="polite"`.
- Citations follow the Dag Hammarskjöld Library's advice: symbol as the key, pinpoint kept, parts formatted on copy.
- Transparency follows OHCHR's "Human Rights-Based Approach to Data": method stated at the point of use (each note at most two sentences), `affected_persons` shown on expand, missing labels shown as missing.

## Out of scope

No model calls and no summaries of what the UN "wants". No comparison with other countries (the file holds one). No follow-up or acceptance status of UPR recommendations (not in the data). No full names of bodies or mandates beyond the `body` label. No regional groups of recommending States. No server, no login, no PDF rendering.

## Sources consulted

- Dag Hammarskjöld Library, Ask DAG: how should I cite a UN document? — https://ask.un.org/faq/401380
- UK Government Analysis Function, Data visualisation: charts (formatting, labels, bar charts) — https://analysisfunction.civilservice.gov.uk/policy-store/data-visualisation-charts/
- UK Government Analysis Function, Data visualisation: tables — https://analysisfunction.civilservice.gov.uk/policy-store/data-visualisation-tables/
- OHCHR, A Human Rights-Based Approach to Data (guidance note) — https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/Documents/Issues/HRIndicators/GuidanceNoteonApproachtoData.pdf

prompts.title: Paragraphs out of a UN document
prompts.prompt:
Build this app. Follow the plan below; where it says nothing, keep it simple. # Paragraphs out of a UN document: the numbered paragraphs of a General Comment, from its HTML, checked against the reference ## Context The user works in an office that quotes UN documents and copies each paragraph by hand. OHCHR's treaty body database serves the document as HTML, which splits cleanly into paragraphs but has lost things on the way. This app turns `WORKSHOP_DATA.html_doc` into numbered paragraphs with the heading each sits under, compares the result with the document's own reference, says plainly what this HTML version lacks, and lets the office take the paragraphs away as a dataset. The document is `html` (a string: parse it with `new DOMParser().parseFromString(html, 'text/html')`); the yardstick is `reference` (`paragraphs`, `footnotes`, `adopted`, `first_words`); `title`, `symbol`, `doc_url` and `source` describe it; nothing is typed in by hand. ## What I found in the data These numbers are from the file I examined; the app computes its own. - One document, 71,380 characters of HTML; `reference.paragraphs` 90, `reference.footnotes` 141, `reference.first_words` keyed by the paragraph number as a string. - **Elements.** A cover `` (the symbol broken over a ``), then `
`: a bold `

` with the committee's name, the title as an `

` ending in " *", 6 roman-numbered `

`, 24 `

` (4 lettered, 20 plain, "Right to work (art. 6)") and 90 numbered `

`; 97 `

` in all. - **Paragraph numbers are glued to the text**: all 90 read "1.A clean…", none "1. A clean". Heading labels too, in 8 of 10 ("I.Introduction"; "D. Obligation" has its space). - **Spaces are missing inside the text.** 23 sentence joins ("levels.Key"), 8 comma joins ("land,wetlands"), 2 quote joins ("crises“increase"), 2 dash joins ("challenges –to"): 35 places in 24 paragraphs that a rule can prove. And word pairs no rule can see: "Giventhe", "Partiesto", "11(2)(a)". The first-words check catches 6 paragraphs (13, 18, 19, 30, 41, 60), only in their first six words. - **Nothing of the footnotes survives**: no footnote text, no footnote marks (the PDF has "waste.2", this file "waste."), and the title's asterisk points to a note that is not in the file. - **Characters a reader does not expect** (kept as published; the first-words check normalises them): 8 non-breaking hyphens (U+2011, "business‑related") beside 106 ordinary ones; 26 en dashes; 20 right single quotes; 5 pairs of curly quotes; 2 non-breaking spaces inside headings. Correct typography that a search typed on a keyboard misses. - Paragraphs are 42 to 253 words of plain prose. ## The app, tab by tab The arrangement of the workshop's Verbatim finder, with two tabs: a reader who sees such a tool for the first time needs the result and the paragraphs, and everything else stays one click away, closed. **Header, always visible.** A monospace label "UN DOCUMENT · HTML", the serif `title`, one line: `symbol` linked to `doc_url` (new tab), "adopted `reference.adopted`", `source`. At the right a green dot "n of m checks pass" or a red dot "n checks failed", then "1 source limit" (the footnotes). **Left rail, always visible.** Headed "DOCUMENT": a card with `symbol` in monospace and the short title. Two big serif numbers: "n paragraphs of `reference.paragraphs`" with a thin bar (red when short or over); "0 footnotes of `reference.footnotes`" in red, "not in this HTML". Then "n of m checks pass". Under the header, numbered tabs (`role="tablist"`, arrow keys): `01 RESULT · 02 PARAGRAPHS`. **01 RESULT. Did the app find everything the document has?** Four tiles, big serif numbers, a "How this is computed" line each: **Paragraphs found: n** beside **the document has `reference.paragraphs`** (green when equal, red with the difference); **First words match: n of `reference.paragraphs`**; **Footnotes: 0 of `reference.footnotes`**, in red, "this HTML version has none: no footnote text, no footnote marks. To cite a footnote, use the PDF or Word version."; **Spaces: n** in n paragraphs. When first words differ, the paragraphs concerned are listed under the tiles, one line each, "para. n: found … / reference …" (at most ten lines, then "and n more"). Under them **Take the paragraphs away**: Two buttons: **Download JSON** and **Download Markdown**. The JSON file is an array of records, each with `symbol`, `paragraph` (its number), `section` and `part` (the nearest heading and the roman-numbered section above it), `text`, `text_raw`, `first_words_match`, `citation`, `doc_url` and `limitations` ("no footnotes in this HTML version; the document has n"). The Markdown file opens with front matter between `---` lines (`title`, `symbol`, `adopted`, `source_url`, `extracted`: today's date, `paragraphs_found`, `paragraphs_expected`, `footnotes`: the same sentence), then the headings as `##` and `###` lines in document order and each paragraph as its number in bold, then its text. File names: the symbol with slashes replaced by hyphens; a Blob URL, UTF-8. Last, two closed headings, buttons with `aria-expanded`: **Every check (m)**, the check panel described below, one line per check; and **The spaces restored (n)**: Paragraph | Before | After | Rule, the count per rule above it (sentence, comma, quote, dash join); clicking a row opens the paragraph on tab 02. Under it: "Rules restore a space only where the characters prove it was there. Word pairs such as 'Giventhe' are not touched." Nothing else on the tab: at most seven things to click. **02 PARAGRAPHS. What does each paragraph say, and how do I cite it?** One row per paragraph: No. | Section | First line | Check. **Section** is the nearest heading above the paragraph ("Right to work (art. 6)"); the expanded row shows the full path ("IV. … › Right to work (art. 6)"). A closed "Headings found: n" box above the table lists them, so none can hide inside a paragraph. First line: the first 120 characters cut at a word with "…"; Check: "OK" or "first words differ" (red). Rows are buttons with `aria-expanded`; click or Enter expands the row in place: the full text, verbatim, never shortened; the reference's six words beside the found six; the places where a space was missing in this paragraph, marked; and a **Copy citation** button that copies "`symbol`, para. n" ("E/C.12/GC/27, para. 12") and shows "Copied" for two seconds; the same string is the `citation` field of every export. **Footer, always visible.** `source`, `built`, and "Done by this page's code; no model was called and nothing left the browser." ## How every number is computed The pipeline runs once on load, over the parsed document's `body` elements in order. - **Classification.** Walk every `table`, `p`, `h2` and `h3` element in document order (`doc.body.querySelectorAll('table, p, h2, h3')`), not only the body's children: everything after the cover sits inside `

`. Elements inside the first `

` are cover. After it, a `

` whose text matches `/^(\d{1,3})\.\s*(.*)$/s` is a paragraph with that number; the first `

` is the title; every other `

` and `

` is a heading, split by `/^([IVX]+|[A-Z])\.\s*(.+)$/` into `label` and `heading` when it matches; any other `

` is the committee line. - **Paragraph text.** `text_raw` = the text after the number and full stop, trimmed, runs of whitespace collapsed to one space. - **Repairs.** `text` = `text_raw` with a space inserted after a full stop between a lowercase and a capital letter (`/([a-z])\.([A-Z])/g` → "$1. $2"), after a comma between letters (`/([a-z]),([A-Za-z])/g`), before an opening curly quote touching a letter (`/([a-z])“/g`) and after an en dash touching a letter (`/–([A-Za-z])/g`). Each insertion is logged with the paragraph, the rule and 20 characters each side; nothing else changes. - **Section** = the nearest heading above the paragraph; `part` = the nearest roman-numbered `

`. A heading is never paragraph text. - **First words.** The first six whitespace-separated words of `text` against `reference.first_words[String(number)]`: equal after turning curly quotes straight, en dashes and non-breaking hyphens into a hyphen and non-breaking spaces into spaces; case is kept. - **Citation** = `symbol` + ", para. " + the paragraph number, with `symbol` read from `WORKSHOP_DATA.html_doc`, never typed in. - **Counts** are loops in JavaScript; nothing is estimated, no model is called. ## How the app checks itself Shown under **Every check** on tab 01, closed until opened. One line per check: what was compared, the two values, and "pass" in green, "check failed" in red with a link to the rows concerned, or "source limit" in red for what the source cannot give. A failed check never hides a result. - **Paragraph count.** Found against `reference.paragraphs`. - **Numbering.** Exactly 1 to n in order; gaps and duplicates listed. - **First words.** Mismatches counted; listed under the tiles of tab 01, the row flagged on tab 02. - **Footnotes.** 0 against `reference.footnotes`: "source limit", with "the HTML version has no footnotes: a limit of the source, not of the app", counted apart from failures. - **Repairs.** n spaces restored in n paragraphs, counted per rule; every one is listed under its closed heading on tab 01, and `text_raw` still holds the text as found. - **Headings.** How many `

` and `

`, and how many glued labels were separated. - **Nothing lost.** Every block element is classified exactly once and the counts per class sum to the total; any unclassified element is listed in red. - **Export round trip.** The JSON to download is parsed back; its record count equals the table's. ## Edge cases and risks - A number glued to its text and one followed by a space are both accepted (`\s*`): this file has 90 of the first, none of the second; another file may be the reverse. - A rule may insert a space only where the characters prove one was there. "Giventhe" stays, caught only when it falls in a paragraph's first six words; a reader who quotes a paragraph still reads it. - The reference is a yardstick, not the truth: when the counts disagree, the app shows both and never trims or pads its result to match. - If `reference` or one of its fields is missing, the tiles say "no reference in this file" and the checks that need it show "not run", never "pass"; if `html` yields no `

`, tab 01 says so and the exports are disabled. ## Design and accessibility What this app adds to the studio look: - **Red accent** on the active tab, the paragraph numbers, the footnotes tile and the words "first words differ", "check failed" and "source limit"; "pass" dark green: words as well as colours. - **Big serif numbers** only on the rail and the tiles of tab 01. Every table has a serif `

` stating the message ("90 paragraphs found, 90 expected"), a monospace number (`TAB.01`), `
`, numbers right-aligned. - A repaired or flagged place is marked in the expanded paragraph by a thin red box. - The check panel follows "Quality assurance of code for analysis and research: Testing code" (Analysis Function): each check tells a story, given this data, having run this code, we expect this output; every damage found has a named check. - The exports follow The Turing Way's "Documentation and metadata": a dataset travels with its source, its fields and its known limitations. - Citations follow the Dag Hammarskjöld Library's "How should I cite a UN document?": fields stored apart and formatted on copy, the symbol as the key, the paragraph as the pinpoint. - Keyboard: rows and closed headings are buttons with `aria-expanded`; a hidden tab panel is not focusable. ## Out of scope No footnote extraction: the source has none. No model calls, no summaries, no comparison with the PDF text, no editing in the browser, one document. ## Sources consulted - The Turing Way, Documentation and metadata — https://github.com/the-turing-way/the-turing-way/blob/bcd8050eed319acc55f8ce0fe0410db157a17f04/book/website/reproducible-research/rdm/rdm-metadata.md - UK Government Analysis Function, Quality assurance of code for analysis and research: Testing code — https://github.com/best-practice-and-impact/qa-of-code-guidance/blob/fa39f2089905fe07c08ae4d66671736a1becd3c5/book/testing_code.md - Dag Hammarskjöld Library, Ask DAG: how should I cite a UN document? — https://ask.un.org/faq/401380

prompts.title: Verbatim finder for General Comments
prompts.prompt:
Build this app. Follow the plan below; where it says nothing, keep it simple.

# Verbatim finder: exact paragraphs of General Comments, with a citation to paste

## Context

The user drafts submissions: a shadow report, an amicus brief, a statement to a treaty body. The reader will check every quotation against the General Comment, so a paraphrase or a wrong paragraph number costs credibility. Today the words come from OHCHR's site or a PDF, copied by hand, or from a chatbot that invents paragraph numbers that sound right. This app searches `WORKSHOP_DATA.gc`, the treaty bodies' General Comments and General Recommendations paragraph by paragraph, with Boolean operators and exact phrases; shows the matching paragraphs as stored; copies a citation built only from the record's fields; and collects quotations for the draft. It retrieves; it never generates. No model is called and nothing leaves the browser.

## What I found in the data

Numbers are from the file I examined; the app computes its own from `records` at load.

- 7,304 records, every field filled except `cited_articles` (2,398). `records.length` is the count; the top-level `count` is the string "7304".
- A symbol is not a document: 159 distinct `symbol`, 188 distinct `title`. 28 symbols are annual reports (A/48/18) or pages of HRI/GEN/1/Rev.9, and 14 hold more than one General Comment; A/48/18 holds seven, so "A/48/18, para. 3" alone is ambiguous.
- Three joint General Comments carry two symbols in one `symbol` ("CMW/C/GC/7–CERD/C/GC/38", en dash; "CRC/C/GC/23, CMW/C/GC/4", comma) but one `committee`.
- `paragraph` runs 0 to 135. 33 records have `paragraph` 0: preambles of early CEDAW and CERD General Recommendations. 22 records are lettered sub-paragraphs ("(a) To take note…") that the file numbers 1, 2, 3.
- 4,258 texts begin with their own number ("12. The Committee…"), 3,046 do not; in 5 the number differs from `paragraph` (three in CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.5, numbered 3.1, 3.2 in the original). Two pinpoints occur twice (CEDAW/C/GC/27 para. 9; the joint GR 31/GC 18 para. 31).
- Footnote marks are written `[[fn:N]]`: 3,238 in 1,857 paragraphs, 212 between two words of a sentence, so the string "Education For All. By virtue" does not exist although the sentence does.
- Quotes are curly: 3,169 curly double quotes against 82 straight; 2,938 curly apostrophes against 78 straight; 248 en dashes, 107 non-breaking spaces; "non-State" 145 times.
- 40 paragraphs contain line breaks; 208 end with a colon and their list sits in the following records. Length 4 to 1,287 words. 10 `committee` codes (CRC 2,091 … CED 56; CAT-OP is the Subcommittee on Prevention of Torture); `year` 1972–2026. `cited_articles` is a third filled and 131 entries start with "?": not offered as a filter.

## The app, tab by tab

Four questions, one per numbered tab; every tab reads the same filtered set.

**Header (always visible).** A small monospace label "UN TREATY BODIES · GENERAL COMMENTS"; the title in serif, "Verbatim finder: General Comments and General Recommendations"; one line: "`records.length` paragraphs from n General Comments (distinct `title`) of k committees, `year` min–max", `source` linked to `source_url`. At the right a green dot and "n checks pass", or a red dot and "n checks failed" (and a red dot on tab 04).

**Left rail (always visible except on the Draft tab).** Headed "FILTERS", with "Clear all". One big serif number, "279 matching paragraphs" (`aria-live`), "of 7,304". Under it the search: a labelled input and a "Search" button; Enter searches. While the box is empty and has focus, a short list opens under it with the syntax in the app's own words (*a space or AND joins words; OR; NOT or a leading minus; "an exact phrase" in double quotes; parentheses; a star at the end of a word for any ending (child\* finds children); operators in capitals, lower-case "or" is a word*) and three examples as options that fill and run: `"best interests" AND child`, `(torture OR ill-treatment) NOT detention`, `"reasonable accommodation"`; it closes when typing starts. One line under the box: "Whole words, any case. Curly and straight quotes, apostrophes, dashes and hyphens count as the same, and footnote marks are skipped, so State's finds State’s and a phrase can cross a footnote." After a search, a line echoes the query as understood: "Paragraphs containing the phrase “best interests” and the word child". An unbalanced quote or parenthesis shows a message and no results. Then one numbered heading, closed until clicked: **01 Committee, years, document**. Committee: a checkbox per code with its full name and, after a search, its hits in brackets; all ticked; "all / none". A joint General Comment (two symbols in one `symbol`) appears when either committee is ticked and shows both badges; the chart's note says "Joint General Comments count under both committees, so the bars can add up to more than the hits". Years: from and to inputs preset to the data's min and max. Document: a select of `short_title` grouped by committee, blank for all. A narrowed filter shows as a small removable chip under the big number.

**01 Overview: which committees say this?**
- FIG.01 "Paragraphs per committee": a horizontal bar chart (Chart.js, `indexAxis: 'y'`), one bar per committee, ranked by value, the value at the end of each bar, axis from zero; the canvas has `role="img"` and an `aria-label` stating the numbers, and a small table with the same numbers beside it. Hint: "click a bar = tick that committee alone". "How this is computed: one count per committee over the paragraphs that match the query and filters."
- Nothing else on this tab. Clickable: 4 tabs, search box, 1 filter heading = 6 (bars are marks, duplicated by the checkboxes).

**02 Paragraphs: what exactly does it say?**
- A summary line (`aria-live`): "279 of 7,304 paragraphs match · 8 committees · 1990–2023", then the order: "sorted by year, newest first, then by document and paragraph"; a select beside it offers document order and most matches first. Under it, one monospace hint: "This page retrieves; it never writes. Every paragraph shown is a record of the file, as stored."
- Results, 25 per page, "Show 25 more". Each row: committee badge and `short_title`; `symbol` linked to `doc_url` in a new tab, the pinpoint ("para. 18", "preamble", "subpara. (b)") and `year`. The text is shown with the footnote marks removed, as it reads in print; a grey line under it says "3 footnote marks removed · show as stored", and that link swaps in the stored `text` character for character. Every matched word or phrase is wrapped in `<mark>` (bold, pale yellow, dark text). Paragraphs up to 700 characters are shown whole; longer ones show the first 700 cut at a word, with "Show the full paragraph (1,287 words)"; `white-space: pre-wrap` keeps stored line breaks. An amber note sits on the row when needed: "the text begins ‘45.’ but the record is para. 41: check the document"; "a lettered sub-paragraph, numbered 2 by the file"; "two records share this pinpoint"; "joint General Comment".
- A click on a row opens it in place, with three buttons and a "Context: previous | next" link. **Copy citation** copies "CCPR/C/GC/37, para. 12"; when the symbol is shared by several General Comments (A/48/18, a page of HRI/GEN/1/Rev.9) the committee and the document's number come first: "CERD, General Recommendation No. 29 (A/57/18), para. 3". A grey note names the style, "UN short form". **Copy quotation** copies the shown text in quotation marks, a space, the citation. **Add to draft** sends both to the Draft tab. "Context" opens paragraph −1 or +1 of the same `title` inline, in grey, with its own pinpoint, for a chapeau that ends in a colon.
- Clickable: 4 tabs, the search box, 1 filter heading, the order select, "Show 25 more" = 8. Row buttons appear only on the open row.

**03 Draft: what have I collected?**
- "Your draft (n quotations)", each with its quotation as copied, its citation and a remove button. The tab name carries the count: "03 DRAFT (4)".
- "Copy all" (quotation, new line, citation, blank line between items); "Download .txt" and "Download .csv" (`citation`, `symbol`, `paragraph`, `pinpoint`, `committee`, `short_title`, `year`, `text_copied`, `text_as_stored`, `doc_url`; UTF-8 with byte-order mark, fields double-quoted).
- A hint says where it is kept: `localStorage` when allowed, in memory otherwise. Clickable: 4 tabs, 3 buttons = 7.

**04 Check & method: can I trust this?**
- The checks panel from "How the app checks itself", open: one line each, "pass" in green or "check failed" in red.
- "Known quirks of this file", computed at load and shown before any search.
- Below, "How this is computed": the next section in short form. Clickable: 6.

**Footer (always visible, one line, small monospace).** `source` and `built`; "Counting, matching and sorting are done by this page's code; no model is called." A Credits line if shelf code is reused (Chart.js, MIT).

## How every number is computed

- **Load.** `R = WORKSHOP_DATA.gc.records`; totals are `R.length`, the sets of `title` and `committee`, the min and max of `year`. Per record, once: `norm`, `marks`, `leading` (`^(\d{1,3})\.\s` on `text`), pinpoint, citation, `shared` (the symbol holds more than one `title`), `joint`, committees.
- **Normalised text** `norm`, once per record at load = `text` with `[[fn:N]]` removed; “ ” „ → "; ‘ ’ ‚ → '; en dash, em dash and soft hyphen → "-"; non-breaking space and all other whitespace, line breaks included, → one space; lower case. The query is normalised the same way, so curly quotes pasted from Word still make a phrase.
- **Query parser.** Tokens: a phrase in double quotes (straight or curly); `(` `)`; `AND`, `OR`, `NOT` in capitals; a leading `-` as NOT; any other run of non-space characters as a word, trailing `*` allowed. Adjacent terms are joined by AND. Precedence NOT, AND, OR; parentheses override. The parser returns a tree and an English echo, or the error shown in the box.
- **Term match.** A word becomes a regular expression over `norm`: the word escaped, trailing `*` → `\w*`, boundaries that work for accented letters, `(?<![\p{L}\p{N}])` before and `(?![\p{L}\p{N}])` after, flag `u`. A hyphen is a boundary, so "state" finds "non-State". A phrase is its words joined by `\s+` inside the same boundaries. A record matches when the Boolean tree is true over `norm`; a NOT-only query matches everything that lacks the terms, and the echo says so.
- **Highlight.** The same terms become a second regular expression over the shown text, where a quote or apostrophe matches its straight and curly forms, a hyphen matches hyphen, en and em dash, and a gap between phrase words matches `(?:\s|\[\[fn:\d+\]\])+`; matches are wrapped in `<mark>` after HTML-escaping. NOT terms are never highlighted.
- **Hits** = records whose tree matches and that pass the committee, year and document filters. **Hits per committee** = one count per committee over the hits, by each record's committee:
- **A record's committees** = the codes found in `symbol` (`\b(CAT|CCPR|CED|CEDAW|CERD|CESCR|CMW|CRC|CRPD)\b`, "CAT-OP" for `CAT/OP`) plus `committee`; the filter keeps a record if any is ticked, and the chart adds it to each of its committees' bars.
- **Shown and copied text** = `text` with every `[[fn:N]]` removed (`\[\[fn:\d+\]\]`, global); `marks` = the number removed. Line breaks, non-breaking spaces and curly quotes stay.
- **Leading number.** When `leading` equals `paragraph`, the copied quotation drops the "12. " at the start (the citation carries the number); the shown text keeps it. When they differ, nothing is dropped and the row carries the amber note.
- **Citation** = `symbol` + ", " + pinpoint. Pinpoint: "para. " + `paragraph`; "preamble" when `paragraph` is 0; "subpara. (b)" when `text` starts with a lettered label (`^\(([a-z]{1,4})\)`). When the symbol is shared by more than one `title` (computed at load), prefix `committee` + ", " + the document's name (`title` up to the first colon or " on ") and put the symbol in parentheses.
- **Copy** uses `navigator.clipboard.writeText`; if refused, the text goes into a selectable box with "Select and copy". After every copy an `aria-live` message shows the exact string sent.
- **Order** = `year` descending, then `title`, then `paragraph` ascending. The select swaps the comparator; the hit set does not change.

## How the app checks itself

Each check is one line: what was compared, the values, "pass" in green or "check failed" in red with the pinpoints concerned. A failed check marks rows; it never drops them.

- **Query understood.** The English echo and the number of terms; a parse error appears here too.
- **Totals.** Rows listed across pages equal the hits; the checkboxes' bracketed counts sum to the hits plus joint hits.
- **Chart total.** The bars sum to the hits plus the joint hits, both shown.
- **Highlight.** Every hit shows at least one `<mark>` unless the query is NOT-only; a hit matched in `norm` but without a highlight is listed as "matched, not highlighted" and still shown.
- **Normalisation.** When the query holds a straight quote, apostrophe or hyphen, the panel says the curly and dash forms were matched too, and how many hits contain only those forms.
- **Numbering.** Hits whose leading number differs from `paragraph`, with both numbers; hits that share a pinpoint with another record of the same `title`; hits that are lettered sub-paragraphs.
- **Marks.** For every hit, the marks removed equal the count of `[[fn:` in the stored `text`, and putting them back gives the stored text exactly.
- **Draft.** For every item, the stored `text` of the record with that `id` is looked up again and compared with the item's `text_as_stored`; a difference marks the item.
- **Known quirks of this file**, computed at load and shown before any search: records with `paragraph` 0, symbols shared by several documents, joint documents, duplicated pinpoints, leading-number mismatches, each with its count and an example.

## Edge cases and risks

- The app can only return paragraphs that exist, with their real `symbol` and `paragraph`; citation and quotation are built from fields, and the Check & method tab says so.
- Preambles are cited as "preamble", never "para. 0"; lettered sub-paragraph records as "subpara. (b)" with a reminder to verify; shared symbols carry the General Recommendation's number, or a reader lands in a 200-page report.
- A leading number that differs from `paragraph` is never corrected: the row shows both.
- Older General Comments may be replaced by later ones (Human Rights Committee GC 36 replaced GC 6 and 14); the file has no "replaced" field, so `year` is on every row.
- Whole words: "child" does not find "children"; the syntax line says to type child\*. Lower-case "or" is a word.
- Long paragraphs are cut on screen only; copy and draft take the whole text. Clipboard or `localStorage` can be refused in a sandbox: the fallback box and memory are always there.
- An empty query with filters lists every paragraph that passes them, paged, and the summary says "no search words".

## Design and accessibility

On top of the studio look:

- **Red accent** on the active tab, the ticked committees and filter chips, the pinpoints ("para. 18") and the bars of FIG.01. Other colours: the `<mark>` highlight (also bold), amber for numbering notes, green for "pass", each also a word.
- **Big numbers:** the matching count in the rail (40–56 px serif). Committee badges are plain outlined monospace labels, one colour.
- **Figure title:** "FIG.01 Paragraphs per committee".
- The chart follows "Data visualisation: charts (formatting, labels, bar charts)" (UK Government Analysis Function): gaps narrower than a bar, at most ten light gridlines, horizontal labels.
- The canvas follows "Chart.js: Accessibility of canvas charts": `role="img"`, an `aria-label` that states the numbers, fallback content, and a visible table with the same values.
- The syntax follows "Wikipedia Help:Searching": double quotes for a phrase, a leading hyphen for exclusion, capital OR, a star for endings; the help text is written fresh, since that page is CC BY-SA.
- Citations follow "Dag Hammarskjöld Library, Ask DAG: how should I cite a UN document?": parts stored separately and formatted on copy, the symbol as the key, a pinpoint always, the style named on screen, no symbol or URL ever invented.
- Keyboard: the search box has focus on load; the example list opens with the arrow keys; rows are `<article>`s with a heading; the count, the summary line and the "Copied" message are `aria-live="polite"`; the chart's click is duplicated by the checkboxes.

## Out of scope

No model calls, summaries or "similar paragraphs". No stemming or synonyms beyond the star. No tracking of which General Comment replaced which. No filter on `cited_articles`. No concluding observations or views, no languages other than English, no editing of texts.

## Sources consulted

- Dag Hammarskjöld Library, Ask DAG: how should I cite a UN document? — https://ask.un.org/faq/401380
- Wikipedia Help:Searching: exact phrase, exclusion, wildcards, AND / OR / NOT and field operators — https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Help:Searching&oldid=1379184667
- Chart.js: Accessibility of canvas charts — https://github.com/chartjs/Chart.js/blob/71d44219e79e3ac41e6f9dc907022eebf574868d/docs/general/accessibility.md
- UK Government Analysis Function, Data visualisation: charts (formatting, labels, bar charts) — https://analysisfunction.civilservice.gov.uk/policy-store/data-visualisation-charts/
prompts.problem: When I draft a submission I need the exact words of General Comments on my topic, a correct citation, and a place to collect the passages I want. Help me find them.

prompts.title: A research wiki on neurotechnology and justice
prompts.prompt:
Build this app. Follow the plan below; where it says nothing, keep it simple.

# Research wiki workspace: neurotechnology in the administration of justice

## Context

A team of human rights professionals follows what ten documents say about neurotechnology in the justice system. The wiki in `WORKSHOP_DATA.wiki` is their compiled knowledge: 40 pages written by models, every claim pinned to a passage of `WORKSHOP_DATA.library` with a verbatim quote. What goes wrong today is upkeep and trust: a new report arrives and nobody reads it into the pages; a chatbot's answer cannot be checked; a report that quotes a General Comment gets cited as if it were one. This app is the workspace: read and navigate, ask the wiki and file good answers back, ingest the waiting document with a person approving each change, and lint. The model drafts; the code verifies every quotation; a person decides. Nothing is called on page load; every call to the model is announced with what leaves the browser.

## What I found in the data

Numbers are from the files I examined; the app computes its own at load.

- 40 pages: 9 source, 14 concept, 14 entity, 3 question; 39 `status` "reviewed", 1 "stub" (`a-hrc-57-61`, an entity page for the inbox document, 11 pins all to other documents, 16 pages linking to it, a ten-item list of what the ingest should check).
- 707 pins, all marked ✓, the number the index states. 625 quotes are whole; 82 join fragments of one passage with "…". A substring check fails those 82; the fragment rule below verifies all 707. Every label matches a passage on its page: "para. N" where the passage has `paragraph` (323 pins), "p. label" where it does not (384).
- Pins per document: A/81/351 227, AHRC-2025 146, UNODC-INTERPOL-2025 78, FuturesLab-2026 75, Szoszkiewicz-Yuste-2025 68, CCPR/C/GC/32 45, CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.4 26, CCPR/C/GC/34 25, Prainsack-et-al-2022 17, A/HRC/57/61 0.
- Six `contested` blocks, one each on six concept pages; the tensions register has the same six cards and five discrepancies of fact. Verdicts: leans-contest 3, contested 2, leans-support 1.
- Links: no dangling `[[slug]]`, no orphan page, `frontmatter.sources` equals the set of pinned documents on every page; `frontmatter.links` and body links differ on 5 entries.
- Sizes: bodies 3,980 to 23,216 characters (median 8,210), 347,911 in all, about 87,000 tokens: no single call can carry the wiki. Index 6,990 characters, log 7,893, tensions 5,568, schema 12,446. Markdown used: headings to `###`, bold, italic, bullets, numbered lists, `[[slug]]`, pins, plain links, fenced `contested` blocks; no tables or images.
- Library: 10 documents; `symbol` null for 5; `paragraph` set in the five UN documents, null in the rest; `page_label` can be "3471" or "e773"; curly quotes in 120 passages, a hyphen followed by a space in 6.
- A/HRC/57/61: `status` "inbox", 100 passages on PDF pages 2–20 (the annex is left out), 61,737 characters, paragraphs 1–84, sub-paragraphs as their own passages ("78 (a)" to "80 (f)"); the passage "5 (a)" holds (b) and (c) inside its text; `section` is a broken fragment for two headings. 13 passages mention justice terms; 29 with evidence, torture and the recommendations.

## The app, tab by tab

The app answers five questions, one per tab, and shows only what the open tab needs (Hick's law): **no view shows more than about seven things to click** (tabs, filter headings and buttons, not table rows or links inside a page's text), and what is used rarely sits one click deeper. There is no filter rail: the one filter narrows the page list, so it sits with the list.

**Header (always visible).** Left: a small monospace label "WIKI · neurotechnology and justice", then the title in serif, "Research wiki: neurotechnology in the administration of justice", then one line from the data: "`pages.length` pages (n sources, n concepts, n entities, n questions) · n pins, n verified by this page · `library.records.length` documents, n in the inbox · built `wiki.built`". Right: a quiet monospace strip "Changes this session: n · Calls to the model: m · Passages that left the browser: k" and, under it, "This page has no storage: changes live in it until you download them (tab 05)". Nothing else.

**Tabs.** Under the header: "01 PAGES · 02 ASK · 03 INGEST · 04 CHECK · 05 RECORD", a `role="tablist"` with arrow keys. `location.hash = slug` opens a page on tab 01, so back and forward work. A running step goes on when you change tab; its tab then reads "03 INGEST · running".

**01 PAGES: what does the wiki say?**
- On the left (320 px), one filter box labelled "title, tag or slug" and a big serif "n of 40 pages". Under it the pages listed by type (plain monospace group labels), each with its `title`, register letters and pin count computed by the code; stubs tagged "stub". Before a page is chosen the main column shows the index, rendered like a page.
- The page: its `title`; badges for `type`, register letters with their names (a treaty law … f scholarship), `status`, `updated`; the `tags`. The `body` rendered: headings, bold, italic, lists, paragraphs; `[[slug]]` as a link to that page (a dangling one in red, "no page"); plain links in a new tab; pins as chips; `contested` blocks as cards.
- Below the body: **Links out** (`frontmatter.links`; those absent from the body marked "frontmatter only"), **Linked from** (every page whose body contains `[[this slug]]`) and **Sources** (`frontmatter.sources`, each with the document's `short_title`, `kind`, `year`, `url`, and "inbox" where it is not ingested). One button, **Copy page as markdown** (frontmatter as YAML, then the body).
- **Pins.** A pin is part of its sentence: the page's prose is written around the quotation ("The central ask [pin] ✓, stated also in the summary [pin] ✓"), so the app shows the quote itself, in quotation marks, where the pin stands, and after it a small chip: the label as a button that calls `studio.openSource(id, page, quote)` with the pin's quote, so the studio opens the PDF at that page beside the app with the quoted passage marked; the document's register letter; and the verification the code computed, "✓ verified" in green or "⚠ not found" in amber, in words as well as colour. Where that differs from the mark written in the page, the chip adds "page says ✓" or "page says ⚠". An arrow expands the chip in place: the matching passage's `paragraph` or `page_label` and its first 300 characters, and "Open the PDF page". Never show a pin as its label alone: the sentence would lose its words.
- **Contested cards.** From each fenced block: the claim as heading; the verdict in words ("leans contest") first and large, in serif; the note; the lean bar labelled "descriptive: support n% of weighted positions, weights a 5 · b 4 · c 3 · d 2 · e 1 · f ½; the verdict is the answer"; then the positions as a table with a `caption` (sign in words, register, pin chip, gloss, page link). A link "in the tensions register" (tab 05) when a `###` entry there names this page in `card:`.
- Clickables: 5 tabs, the filter box, Copy page as markdown = 7.

**02 ASK: what does the wiki answer, and is it worth filing?**
- A labelled text box and the button **Ask the wiki** (Enter sends; once there is an answer the same button reads "Ask again"). A grey box above states what each step will send before it goes. Step 1 sends the index and the question; the model returns up to five slugs, shown as chips with a **Change pages** link that lets you tick others. Step 2 sends those pages' bodies, announced as "5 pages, 41,200 characters; 0 library passages have left the browser", and the question. The answer's pins must already stand on the pages sent; one that does not is shown struck through with "not on the pages sent". The answer comes as one text. Each pin chip carries its document's register letter and name ("(c) UN report"), and the prompt says: name the register where it matters, keep the document's own verb, never present (c) to (f) as what the treaty requires. Under the answer, one line counts the verified pins by register.
- The answer is rendered like a page, inside `data-source="ai"`, every pin chip verified by the code, with "What the library cannot answer" from the model's `cannot_answer`. Under it **File as a question page**, which opens the card below in place, with **File this page** and **Copy answer**.
- **Filing a question page.** The card previews the page the code builds: slug from the title (kebab-case, unique), `type` "question", `tags` typed by the user, `register` from the pinned documents, `status` "draft", `updated` today, `links` from the `[[slugs]]` in the answer, `sources` from the pins; body = "# title", "**Short answer.**", "## Reasoning" (the answer), "## What the library cannot answer", "## Related". **File this page** adds it to `pages`, its line to the index under Questions and `## [date] ask | title` to the log. Disabled, with the reason, until every pin in the answer verifies.
- Each step has a progress line and a Stop button (shown while it runs); a parse failure shows the raw answer with "Retry".
- Clickables: 5 tabs, Ask the wiki, File as a question page = 7 (8 once the filing card is open).

**03 INGEST: what would the waiting document change?** Here sit the buttons **Ingest `symbol`** (one per library document whose `status` is "inbox"; `short_title` when `symbol` is null; none, and the line "Nothing waits in the inbox", when it is empty) and, on step 1, **Start**.
- Pressing it opens a stepper of four steps with one running line: "calls so far m · passages sent k"; the button gives way to the stepper.
- **Step 1, scope.** **Scope: the whole document.** The panel says: "All `passages.length` passages will be sent, in batches of 25 (n calls), c characters; nothing is held back." A table lists the batches with their paragraph ranges and PDF pages. **Start** runs them one after another with a progress line ("batch 2 of 4 · 50 of 100 passages have left the browser") and a Stop button that keeps what has returned.
- **Step 2, takeaways.** As each batch returns, a table grows: claim, quote, passage (paragraph and PDF page), the pages it would touch (slugs as chips), and the verification result in words. A box **Could not verify: n** lists each failed quote with the passage the model named, the nearest passage on that page and an **Open the PDF page** button; these claims are in no change card and in no later prompt.
- **Step 3, drafts.** "Draft the source page (1 call)" sends the verified takeaways; the draft appears as a change card. Then "Draft the changes to n pages (n calls)" runs one call per touched page with a progress line and Stop; the stub `a-hrc-57-61` is always among them, rewritten with its ten-item checklist sent along.
- **Step 4, review and file.** Each change is one page: a card with the page's title and type, "new page" or "edited", the number of paragraphs inserted and pins added (verified and not, in words), then the page shown with every inserted paragraph on a pale yellow background and the rest in grey, pins as chips. Two buttons, **Approve this page** and **Reject this page**, and a line "change 3 of 9". Nothing is written until Approve is pressed; a rejected page stays exactly as loaded and the rejection is noted in the log entry. After the last decision, **File the approved changes** writes them at once: pages replaced or added with `updated` today; the index updated (see "Index line" below); `## [date] ingest | symbol: short_title` appended to the log; any new contested card added to the tensions register; the document's `status` set to "ingested" in memory; Lint re-run. Until then nothing in the wiki changes.
- Clickables: 5 tabs plus the Ingest button, or Start, or one draft button, or the two decision buttons of the open change card = 6 to 7 (8 with the per-claim buttons).

**04 CHECK: can I trust this?**
- At the top one big serif number, "n of n pins verified by this page", and "n lint checks need a look".
- **Lint.** A table with a `caption` of checks, each with its count and the pages concerned as links: dangling links; orphans; pins not verified by the code; pins marked ✓ that fail; `sources` that differ from the documents pinned; pages with no pins; `links` not reciprocated; pages missing from the index or index lines without a page; index ✓N that differs from the computed count; contested cards without a tensions entry and the reverse; stub pages; pins to a document still in the inbox. Each reads "0 · pass" or "n · check". One button, **Lint now**, which reads "Re-run" after the first run. The schema's reading for contradictions is named on screen as not done by code.
- **Checks panel** (from "How the app checks itself"), open by default, under the table.
- Clickables: 5 tabs, Lint now = 6.

**05 RECORD: what has changed, where do the sources disagree, and how do I take it away?**
- The `log` rendered newest first (a switch flips it), each `## [date] op | subject` collapsible; below it the `tensions` register, each `card:` link opening its page on tab 01. Entries added in this session carry "this session".
- A short method note (counting, matching and verification are done by the page's code; each number has its "How this is computed" line) and the data source line.
- **Download the wiki**, and, once there are changes, a second button that saves the changed pages as one markdown file.
- Clickables: 5 tabs, the order switch, Download the wiki = 7 (8 with the second download).

**Footer (always visible, one line, small monospace).** `wiki.source`, `wiki.built` and "Counting, matching and verification are done by this page's code; the model is called only when you press Ask, Ingest or a retry button."

## How every number is computed

- **Load.** `P = WORKSHOP_DATA.wiki.pages`, `D = WORKSHOP_DATA.library.records`, maps slug → page and id → document. Per page: `bodyLinks` = the slugs in `/\[\[([^\]|#]+)/g`; `pins` = every match of `/\[([^\]]+)\]\(pin:([^#\s)]+)#p(\d+)(?: "([^"]*)")?\) ?(✓|⚠)/g` (label, id, page, quote, mark); `backlinks[slug]` = pages whose `bodyLinks` contain it. Header counts are `P.length`, counts by `type`, pins and verified pins summed, documents with `status` "inbox".
- **Normalise** `norm(s)`: Unicode NFKC; “ ” „ → "; ‘ ’ → '; en and em dash → "-"; soft hyphen removed; a hyphen followed by whitespace → "" ("decision- making" = "decision-making"); runs of whitespace → one space; trimmed. Capitals are kept (the schema says words and capitals must match).
- **verify(pin)** = true when a passage `x` of document `id` with `x.page === page` exists such that the quote, split on "…" or "..." into fragments, has every fragment found in `norm(x.text)` in order, each search starting where the previous fragment ended; and the label contains "para. " + `x.paragraph` when `x.paragraph` is set, otherwise "p. " + `x.page_label`. A pin with no quote, an unknown `id`, or a document whose `status` is "inbox" is not verified, with the reason kept for the chip. The 707 pins of the file I examined all verify by this rule.
- **Cite-as** for a document = the most frequent text before ", para." or ", p." in the existing pins' labels to it; with no pins, its `symbol`, or `author` + " " + `year` when `symbol` is null. **New pin** = `[cite-as, para. <paragraph>](pin:id#p<page> "quote") ✓` (", p. <page_label>" when `paragraph` is null); straight double quotes inside the quote become “ ” first, so the regular expression still matches.
- **Register of a document** = the `register` of the source page whose `sources` is exactly [that id], else of the stub page with that `sources`, else "?". A new page's `register` = the registers of its pinned documents.
- **Contested card** from a block: `claim`, `verdict`, `note` by prefix; a position line splits on " | " into sign, register, pin, gloss, page. **Lean** = (Σ weight of "+" + ½ Σ weight of "~") ÷ Σ weight of all positions, weights a 5, b 4, c 3, d 2, e 1, f 0.5, shown as a percentage with the formula.
- **Calls to the model.** One function for every call: it shows the prompt's size in characters and the passage objects in it, adds both to the session counters, calls `await studio.ask(prompt, {json: true})`, parses JSON (once more after stripping a fenced code block), and on failure shows the raw answer with Retry. Every prompt states the pin syntax and "quote only words that stand in the passages given; the code will check".
- **Ask, call 1** = the index + the question → JSON `{pages: [slug…]}`, kept to slugs that exist, at most 5. **Call 2** = the bodies of the chosen pages + the question → JSON `{title, answer, cannot_answer}`, answer at most 350 words. A pin in the answer is accepted when the same `pin:id#pPAGE` with the same quote exists in a sent page's body and `verify` is true; otherwise it is struck through. Characters sent = the lengths of the strings sent, added up; passages sent = 0.
- **Register of a pin** = the register of its document (above), shown on every chip; the count line is one number per letter over the answer's verified pins.
- **Batches** = the document's `passages` in file order, cut every 25; the number of calls = ceil(n ÷ 25). Every passage is sent exactly once.
- **Takeaway call** (one per batch): the batch's passages as `{id, page, paragraph, text}`, the index, and "return JSON {takeaways: [{claim, quote, passage, pages}]}, at most 10, quote 8 to 40 words copied verbatim from that one passage, pages = slugs from the index the claim bears on". For each takeaway the code finds the passage by `id`, builds the pin and runs `verify`; `pages` are kept to slugs that exist, plus at most two new slugs per ingest, which become "new page" cards.
- **Failed takeaway** = `verify` false. It is kept in `failed[]` with the model's quote and the nearest passage (the passage on that page sharing the longest run of consecutive normalised words with the quote, and that run's length), and excluded from every later prompt.
- **Source page call**: the verified takeaways with their ready-made pins, the cite-as, the document's `title`, `author`, `published`, `pages` and `url`, the schema's source-page anatomy (Full cite, Register, One-liner, Key takeaways, How NOT to read this, Where it feeds the wiki, Related) and "return JSON {one_liner, body, touches: [{slug, why}]}, body at most 900 words, only the pins given, copied exactly". The code re-verifies every pin in `body`, builds the frontmatter itself (`type` "source", `register` from the stub, `sources` [id], `links` from the body, `tags` from the touched slugs) and keeps `touches` to existing or allowed new slugs, at most 12, the stub added if missing.
- **Touched page call** (one per slug): the page's `body`, the takeaways whose `pages` include the slug, with their pins, and "return JSON {edits: [{after, markdown}], contested}, each `after` an existing heading or 'end', at most 300 words in all, pins copied exactly, `contested` a full block only where this document disagrees with the page". The code inserts each `markdown` at the end of the named heading's section (at the end of the page, with a note, when the heading is not found), re-verifies every pin, adds the link both ways in `links` and the document id to `sources`.
- **Index line** = "- [[slug]] — one-liner · (letters) · ✓N", N the verified pins counted by the code; the source page's line goes under Sources, the stub's is replaced, touched pages' N recomputed, the first line rebuilt from the counts. **Log entry**: "Read n passages (cite-as, register (x)). Wrote [[slug]]. N pins in all; besides its own page, pinned on k pages: [[…]]. Rejected: [[…]]." **Tensions entry** for a new card: `### slug-of-claim`, `title`, `status` (contested → open; leans-* → leaning; settled-* → settled), `card: [[page]]`, `poles` and `where` from the positions.
- **Download** = a Blob of JSON in the shape of `WORKSHOP_DATA.wiki` (pages, index, log, tensions, schema, count) plus `changes` (each approved change with date and kind) and `library_status`, saved as `wiki-<date>.json` through a temporary `<a download>`; a second button saves the changed pages as one markdown file with `---` separators.

## How the app checks itself

A panel of one-line checks: what was compared, the values, "pass" in green or "check" in red, with the pages concerned as links. A failing check never hides a page or a pin.

- **Pins.** Pins found by the regular expression against the number stated in the first line of the index (`/(\d[\d,]*) pins/`); verified against found; any ✓ that fails listed with its page.
- **Labels.** Every verified pin's label matches its passage's `paragraph` or `page_label`.
- **Structure.** Dangling links 0; orphans 0; `sources` equal pinned documents on every page; every page in the index and every index `[[slug]]` a page; contested cards equal tensions `card:` entries.
- **Model answers.** For every call: JSON parsed; slugs that do not exist listed; takeaways returned, verified and failed adding up.
- **Coverage.** Passages sent equal `passages.length`; every takeaway's `passage` id is among them; a takeaway naming a passage that was not sent is dropped and counted.
- **Unverified.** After an ingest the count of ⚠ pins in the wiki is unchanged (0 in the file I looked at) and every pin in a changed page verifies; the "could not verify" count plus the verified takeaways equal the takeaways returned.
- **Approval.** Pages changed in the wiki equal approved cards; the log entry lists approved and rejected pages by slug; no page differs from its loaded body without an approved card naming it.
- **Filing.** After filing: the new or changed pages re-parsed and re-verified; the index line count equals the page's verified pins; the log's last entry names the pages changed; Lint re-run and its before and after counts shown side by side.
- **Session.** Changes listed equal the log entries added this session; the download's page count equals `pages.length`.

## Edge cases and risks

- The model may change a quote while "copying" it: every pin is re-verified after every call, never trusted from the mark it wrote. A straight `"` inside a quote would break the pin syntax: the code makes it curly first.
- A sub-paragraph passage ("5 (a)") carries (b) and (c) in its text: the label is the passage's `paragraph` as stored, and the chip shows the passage so a reader sees where the words sit. `section` is broken for two headings of A/HRC/57/61: shown as stored, never used as a heading in a draft.
- Footnotes, tables and captions are not in the passages: a pin cannot verify them; the chip says so.
- A model answer may name a slug that does not exist (dropped and listed) or propose a new page with an existing slug (treated as an edit of that page).
- `studio.ask` can fail or return prose: the raw answer is shown, nothing is filed, Retry re-sends the same prompt; Stop keeps what has returned.
- Everything lives in memory: reloading loses the session, so the warning stays in the header and Download sits on tab 05. The counters show calls and passages before and after each step; a whole ingest of the inbox document is at most about 4 + 1 + 12 calls.
- The lean bar can mislead: the verdict comes first and the bar is labelled descriptive, as the schema requires. Registers are on every chip so a (c) report is never read as (b).

## Design and accessibility

- **What this app adds to the studio look.** Red accent also on the lean bar and the "this session" tag. Big serif numbers: the verified-pin count on tab 04, the running calls and passages on tab 03, the page count on tab 01; the verdict of a contested card is a large serif word. `FIG.01` titles on the lean bar, the takeaways table and the lint table. Category colours only for state, always with words: verified green, not found amber, check red, pass green; register letters stay monospace, not six colours; inserted text on pale yellow with a left border. Tab 01 has two columns (list 320 px, text up to 900 px), one below 900 px.
- From "The A11Y Project checklist": unique, descriptive button labels ("Approve change 3 of 9", "Open A/HRC/57/61 at PDF page 12"); every input has a `<label>`; change cards are a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>`; chips and borders 3:1.
- From the quality-assurance guidance on generative AI (UK Government Analysis Function): nothing a model wrote enters the wiki before a person has read it, and the prompt box says what leaves the browser before it leaves.
- From Karpathy's "LLM Wiki" and the author's schema: the library is read-only; the index is read before pages; the log is append-only; the three operations are the three buttons (Ask, Ingest, Lint now).
- **Keyboard and screen reader.** Focus is on the first tab on load; `aria-live="polite"` on progress lines, counters and the "Filed" message, and on the "running" mark of a tab; Escape stops a running step; nothing opens in a modal. Every model output sits inside `data-source="ai"`.

## Out of scope

No free-text editing of pages by hand. No PDF viewer inside the app (`studio.openSource` opens the page and marks the quote). No search beyond the page filter on tab 01. No version history beyond this session's change list. No lint of contradictions by the model. No ingest of a document that is not in the inbox, and no second ingest of the same document. No export other than JSON and markdown.
